A University of Utah researcher stumbled upon a discovery when cleaning out an office. The find was a computer program from 1974 and thought to be lost forever.

The UNIX v4 had just around 20 copies ever and one made its way to Salt Lake City over 50 years ago. The program was in a tape dispenser and a label, and at first there was no clue if what was on the tape was the real deal.

The program was driven to the Computer History Museum for testing, and the entire program was intact.

The group that made the discovery from the University of Utah joined ARC Salt Lake to discuss the significance of this find and what it means.

Estou experimentando usar o Claude Code pra continuar progredindo na meta de byte-matching do disasm e rebuild das ROMs do KN5000. Aparentemente ele acabou de conseguir consertar 201 bytes. Ainda preciso verificar se é roubadinha, ou se é progresso real.
Os recursos da janela de 5 horas se esgotaram em menos de 2 horas de sessão... kkkk

Essa tarefa consome muitos recursos. Foram corrigidos "apenas" 303 bytes em duas horas de trabalho do Claude Code. (De uma imagem ROM de 2 megabytes que já estava com 99,94% de byte-matching quando eu pedi pro Claude tentar melhorar os scores, então não foi uma tarefa trivial.)
No momento ainda não estou convencido de que é uma boa estratégia. Mas também acho bacana ter tido algum progresso automatizado, mesmo que de forma meio lenta.

Fiz as contas aqui. Plano PRO custa 1100 reais por ano. Essa sessão gastou 13% da minha cota semanal. São 52 semanas em um ano. Então... (13%)/52 * 1100 = R$ 2,75
303 bytes corrigidos por 2 reais e 75 centavos.
Ou pouco mais de 1 centavo por byte :-P
imagino que o ritmo de avanço não seja constante. E até tenha sido mais lento nessa tarefa, por já estar próximo de 100%. Mas tudo isso é especulação.

Se não for possível ter um ritmo melhor, não vale a pena. Pois nesse ritmo, fazer o disasm completo duma ROM de 2Mbytes custaria ridículos 20 mil reais!
Estou no meu primeiro dia de experimentos. Acho que deve ter muitos caminhos possíveis pra se otimizar melhor esse processo e reduzir a taxa de consumo de tokens.
Mas uma coisa eu tenho certeza! Escovar bits e fazer o disasm manualmente é bem mais divertido que operar uma sessão de Claude Code.
Sinto como se eu estivesse roubando nas regras do jogo

3 sessões do Claude Code reduziram de 1310 bytes errados para 177 bytes errados. Ainda não revisei se o que ele está fazendo é correto. Mas, acompanhando o histórico das sessões, muita coisa parece fazer muito sentido!
Assim que ele chegar em 100% vou fazer uma mega revisão do código

text.text: AI hype meets reality as majority of CEOs report no financial returns
Most businesses are still waiting for AI to boost revenue and cut costs

A new PwC survey of 4,454 CEOs from 95 countries shows that 56% have not seen significant financial returns from AI. Despite widespread adoption, AI implementation has led to cost or revenue improvements for only 12% of companies. However, CEOs remain optimistic and continue investing, driven more by the fear of falling behind than proven results. Businesses with strong AI foundations are more likely to see returns, but many AI initiatives are still in early stages and not fully integrated into core operations.

texts.text:
Serving tech enthusiasts for over 25 years. 
TechSpot means tech analysis and advice

Despite being advertised as the holy grail for businesses, embracing AI doesn't mean a company will automatically experience improvements. A new survey that questioned thousands of CEOs found that more than half admit to seeing no significant financial benefit from AI to date.
Professional services network PwC's latest Global CEO
was completed by 4,454 Chief Executive Officers across 95 countries and territories.

text.text: Unsurprisingly, a lot of the questions are related to AI. Most companies have introduced the technology into their businesses to varying extents, but 56% of CEOs say it hasn't produced any cost or revenue benefits.

Some CEOs said that AI had led to cost or revenue improvements: a third said they had seen increased revenue in the last 12 months, while 26% said they are seeing lower costs – but 22% said their costs had actually increased. What might concern those already worried about AI being a bubble is that just 12% of CEOs reported both these positive changes as a result of implementation.

Rather than questioning whether AI is the golden ticket companies like OpenAI claim it to be, PwC's narrative shifts the focus elsewhere: businesses with strong "AI foundations" – including responsible AI frameworks and technology environments that support enterprise-wide integration – are two to three times more likely to report meaningful financial returns, apparently.
In fact, rather than worrying that AI might not live up to the hype, the biggest concern among CEOs is whether they are transforming fast enough to keep pace with technological change.
After decades at HP, CEO Enrique Lores leaves for PayPal in surprising shift
One-third of game industry workers were affected by layoffs in 2025, GDC report finds

That anxiety is backed up by some interesting numbers. According to PwC, 69% of CEOs believe generative AI will require most of their workforce to develop new skills within the next three years, yet fewer than half say their companies have a clear plan in place to reskill employees at scale. It appears many leaders are betting on AI-driven transformation while still figuring out how their people will keep up.

Also, while a large majority of CEOs say AI will fundamentally change how their company creates value, only a minority describe their AI initiatives as fully integrated into core business processes. For many organizations, AI is still stuck in pilot projects, isolated tools, or productivity experiments rather than something that reshapes decision-making or operating models.

PwC's data suggests that CEOs aren't losing faith in AI. Nearly three-quarters expect it to significantly boost profitability over the next 12 months, despite the fact that most haven't seen meaningful gains so far. That optimism may help explain why investment continues to accelerate even as results lag behind expectations.

The survey paints a picture of a AI adoption being driven less by proven returns and more by fear of falling behind. CEOs aren't pulling back because AI doesn't work – they're doubling down because the cost of not transforming fast enough feels even riskier. Whether that confidence is justified, or simply another chapter in the long history of tech hype-driven FOMO, is something the next few years will make painfully clear.

Warning! Lot's of raging and swearing take place in this video, if you have sensitive ears or are easily offended by an over-age man swearing at a 35 year old game, please change the channel.

Donkey Kong is the new champion of closest arcade clone ever done on the Coco... because it is the arcade game. John Kowalski, who came up with the 3D algorithm used in Nick Marentes' Gate Crasher game, hand translated the original Z80 code from the arcade to 6809 code, and then wrote hardware emulation routines to emulate the original graphics and sound hardware. Thus, the entire original arcade game is there - background sound/music, all intermissions, attract mode, etc. The only slight change is to compress the vertical # of pixels for the graphics (from the arcade original's 240 to the Coco 3's maximum of 225). This is the most ambitious game done on the Coco 3 yet. For more details on the game, it's development, and where Coco emulation could go from here, please visit Sock Master's Donkey Kong site, and get the full story right from this genius' own website.

Title: Donkey Kong
Author: John Kowalski (Sock Master) and Nintendo
Publisher: John Kowlaski - Freeware
Released: March 31, 2007
Requires: Color Computer 3, 512K RAM, joystick. A 6309 does make the game run smoother, but is not required.
